before.content_html:
Women of Legend: Ideal and Dangerous

The myths of ancient Greece and Rome are full of extraordinary women — figures whose stories were told and retold because they embodied ideas their cultures found compelling, troubling or both. These legendary women were rarely straightforward. Some represented the ideal: the faithful wife, the devoted mother. Others embodied danger: the sorceress, the adulteress, the woman who stepped beyond her proper boundary. Together they reveal a great deal about what Greek and Roman men feared, admired and expected from women.

Pandora: The First Woman

The Greek poet Hesiod tells the story of Pandora in his poem Works and Days. According to Hesiod, the gods created Pandora as a gift — but a treacherous one. Zeus was angry that Prometheus had stolen fire to give to humanity, so he sent Pandora as punishment. The gods each gave her a quality: beauty, charm, cunning, deceit. She was sent to live with men, carrying a large storage jar (in Greek, a pithos). When she opened it, all the evils, sicknesses and hardships that now afflict humankind poured out into the world. Only Hope remained trapped inside.

Hesiod describes Pandora in deeply ambivalent terms. She is “beautiful evil,” a figure whose loveliness conceals destruction. His account reflects a widespread ancient Greek tendency to blame women for human suffering. For the exam, it is important to move beyond the narrative and ask: what does this myth tell us about how men viewed women? Pandora is passive, curious and dangerous — a combination that justified the supervision and seclusion of real women in Athens.

Key Fact

Hesiod’s Works and Days, lines 53–105, is the prescribed literary source for Pandora. The jar (pithos) she opens releases evils into the world; only Hope remains inside. Pandora embodies the Greek view that women are “beautiful evil” — attractive but destructive.

Helen of Troy

Helen was said to be the most beautiful woman in the world, the daughter of Zeus and Leda. Her abduction — or elopement — with the Trojan prince Paris caused the Trojan War, which resulted in the deaths of thousands and the destruction of a great city. The prescribed literary source for Helen is Euripides’ play Helen, lines 1–67, in which Helen herself speaks. In Homer’s Iliad, Book 3 (lines 121–244), she appears in a scene known as the “viewing from the walls” (the teichoscopia). Lines 121–180 show the goddess Iris visiting Helen in her chamber and leading her to the Scaean Gate; from line 181 onwards, Helen identifies the Greek leaders — Agamemnon, Odysseus, Ajax and Idomeneus — to the Trojan king Priam as they watch from the walls.

Helen is a complex figure. In the Iliad, Homer shows her as deeply conflicted: she condemns herself and longs to return home. In Euripides’ Helen, the playwright invents a radical version of the story in which Helen never went to Troy at all — only her phantom did — and she spent the whole war faithfully waiting in Egypt. This version completely reverses her reputation. The contrast between the two literary treatments is important: it shows how ancient authors could use myth to explore different ideas about female virtue, guilt and agency.

Ancient sources disagree sharply. In Homer’s Iliad, Helen acts with some autonomy but also expresses remorse — she calls herself a “dog” and wishes she had died. In Euripides’ Helen, she is entirely innocent: it is a phantom, not the real Helen, who went to Troy. This version was unusual in antiquity and would have surprised an ancient audience expecting the familiar version. The key point for analysis is that male authors controlled Helen’s story: even her innocence was invented by a man. The Hegeso Stele, a grave relief in Athens dating to around 400 BC, shows a very different kind of woman — the quiet, domestic ideal. The contrast with Helen is striking.

Medea: The Dangerous Foreign Woman

Medea is one of the most terrifying women in Greek myth. The prescribed literary source is Euripides’ play Medea, lines 1–38 and 1293–1389. Medea is a foreigner — a princess from Colchis on the Black Sea — and a powerful sorceress. She used her magic to help Jason win the Golden Fleece and sailed back to Greece with him, killing her own brother to prevent pursuit. When Jason abandons her to marry a Greek princess, Medea’s revenge is catastrophic: she kills their children to punish him most deeply.

The opening of the play (lines 1–38) is narrated by the Nurse, who sets out Medea’s misery and her dangerous, passionate nature. The ending (lines 1293–1389) shows Medea escaping in a chariot drawn by dragons, unpunished. For an Athenian audience, Medea concentrated every fear about foreign women: she was not bound by the social rules that kept Athenian women in their place. She acted independently, used magic and destroyed her own family. The Flight of Medea Krater in the Cleveland Museum of Art, a red-figure vessel dating to around 400 BC, depicts Medea in her dragon chariot, the dead children visible below — confirming that this was a well-known and disturbing image.

Roman authors inherited Greek myths but shaped them to reflect Roman values. The emphasis in Roman storytelling tends to fall more heavily on virtue (virtus), duty (pietas) and service to the state. A dangerous Greek figure like Medea (a foreigner who kills her children) maps onto Roman anxiety about powerful foreign women, a theme that would resurface in the Roman portrayal of Cleopatra. By contrast, Roman legend produced the story of the Sabine Women — a very different treatment of women caught in conflict between loyalties.

The Sabine Women and Tarpeia

The Sabine Women feature in Livy’s History of Rome, 1.9–10 and 1.12–13, one of the prescribed literary sources. The early Romans, all men, lacked wives. Romulus invited the neighbouring Sabines to a festival and seized their women. The Sabine men went to war to reclaim them — but by then the women had settled, married and had children. In Livy’s account, the Sabine women themselves rush between the two armies and plead for peace, declaring that they would rather die than see their fathers and husbands kill each other. Their intervention ends the war.

This myth celebrates a Roman female ideal: self-sacrifice, loyalty to family and the ability to maintain harmony. These women are powerful, but their power is exercised in the service of the community rather than for personal gain. Contrast this with Tarpeia, whose betrayal of Rome for personal reward made her a figure of shame — her name lives on in the Tarpeian Rock, the cliff from which condemned traitors were thrown.

Key Fact

The Sabine Women (Livy 1.9–10, 1.12–13) and Tarpeia represent contrasting Roman attitudes: the Sabine Women’s self-sacrificing intervention models ideal womanhood, while Tarpeia’s treachery for personal gain models the dangerous, selfish woman to be condemned.

Lucretia: The Roman Ideal

The story of Lucretia appears in Livy, 1.57–59. She was renowned for her virtue: while the Roman princes were carousing during the siege of Ardea, Lucretia alone was found at home, weaving with her slave women. This visual image — the weaving wife at home — is the Roman ideal of female virtue made flesh. When Sextus Tarquinius raped her, Lucretia told her father and husband, then killed herself, saying no unchaste woman should ever use her as a precedent. Her death triggered the expulsion of the kings and the founding of the Roman Republic. Lucretia’s story is therefore political as well as moral: her body becomes the site on which Roman political identity is built. The prescribed visual source Pudicitia (Pudicizia) in the Vatican Museum shows a draped female figure whose posture — head slightly bowed, cloak drawn across the body — conveys modesty and self-concealment, the physical embodiment of the virtue Lucretia exemplified.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Greek and Roman myth portrays legendary women across a spectrum: from the ideal (the Sabine Women’s self-sacrifice, Lucretia’s chastity) to the dangerous (Pandora’s curiosity, Medea’s violence, Helen’s beauty).
  • Prescribed literary sources — Hesiod’s Works and Days (lines 53–105 for Pandora), Euripides’ Helen and Medea, Homer’s Iliad Book 3 (lines 121–244 for the teichoscopia), Livy — shape these stories from a male perspective; asking who wrote the source and why is essential for analysis.
  • Material sources such as the Flight of Medea Krater and the Pudicitia statue confirm that both the dangerous and the ideal woman were visually represented, giving us evidence beyond the literary tradition.

before.content_html:
Growing Up Female in the Ancient World

The experience of growing up as a girl in ancient Greece depended enormously on where you lived. Athens and Sparta were both Greek city-states, but they held strikingly different views about what a young woman should become and how she should be prepared for that role. In Athens, a girl was trained for marriage and domesticity. In Sparta, she was trained for physical fitness and the production of strong children for the state. Comparing these two systems is one of the core analytical skills this topic demands.

Growing Up in Athens

Athenian girls did not attend school. Their education took place within the home, overseen by their mother, female relatives and domestic slaves. They learned the skills they would need as wives: weaving, spinning, managing a household and, in wealthier families, basic literacy. The goal was to make them a good wife — obedient, domestic and chaste.

Athenian girls were married young, typically between the ages of fourteen and eighteen, to men who were considerably older, often in their late twenties or thirties. The marriage was arranged not between the couple themselves but between families. The key figure was the kyrios — the woman’s male guardian, usually her father, and after marriage her husband. The kyrios had legal authority over the woman and conducted all negotiations on her behalf, since women in Athens had no legal standing of their own.

Key Fact

In Athens, girls were typically married at fourteen to eighteen to men significantly older than themselves. The marriage was arranged by the girl’s kyrios (male guardian). The girl had no legal voice in the arrangement.

The Athenian Wedding

An Athenian wedding was a structured ritual spread over several days. Before the ceremony, the bride dedicated her childhood toys, her kalyptra (bridal veil) and often a lock of her hair to the goddess Artemis, marking the end of girlhood. The ceremonial lifting of the veil by the groom was called the anakalypteria. On the evening of the wedding, the bride bathed in sacred water brought from the spring Enneakrounos; she was dressed and adorned; and a procession (the nuptial torch-lit procession) carried her by cart or on foot from her father’s house to her new husband’s home. Friends and relatives accompanied the couple, singing hymns. The transfer of the bride from one household to another was the central act: the woman was passing from the authority of her father to the authority of her husband.

A central part of the marriage arrangement was the dowry. The bride’s father paid a sum of money or property to the groom. In law this remained the wife’s property, but in practice the husband controlled it. If the marriage ended in divorce, the dowry had to be returned. This financial arrangement meant that daughters were a significant economic commitment for their fathers, and poorer families sometimes had difficulty securing marriages for their daughters. The pyxis — a small, lidded box used for cosmetics and trinkets — was a common wedding gift in Athens, and several fine examples survive. One notable example, the Gold pyxis from Shaft Grave V at Mycenae (now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens), shows how far back the idea of decorative personal containers for women extends.

Beyond the financial dowry, a woman brought her domestic skills, her reputation for modesty and her capacity to produce legitimate heirs. Athenian citizenship law (under Pericles, 451 BC) required that both parents be Athenian citizens for a child to inherit full citizen rights. This gave every Athenian man a strong interest in his wife’s fidelity, since only a legitimate, citizen-born wife could produce citizen sons. The seclusion of women within the home (the gynaikon) was partly a response to this legal requirement: it was a way of policing female sexuality and guaranteeing the legitimacy of children.

Growing Up in Sparta

Sparta’s approach to raising girls was radically different. In Sparta, girls participated in public physical education alongside boys. They ran, wrestled, threw the discus and javelin, and competed in athletic festivals. This was deeply shocking to other Greeks. The Athenian writer Plutarch, in his life of the Spartan lawgiver Lycurgus (not a prescribed source, but useful context), remarked that this regime made Spartan women more physically robust and better prepared for childbirth.

The purpose of this education was not to make Spartan women independent; it was to make them produce healthy, strong sons for the Spartan army. Sparta’s entire social system was organised around the production of warriors. Girls who were physically fit were expected to survive childbirth more easily and to carry children well. Spartan women also married later than Athenian women, typically in their late teens or early twenties, to men of similar age — the theory was that both partners should be mature and at physical peak for breeding. This produced a very different dynamic from the typical Athenian age gap.

Key Fact

Spartan girls received public physical training — running, wrestling, athletics — to produce healthy children for the state. They married later (late teens to early twenties) than Athenian girls (fourteen to eighteen). Spartan women could own property and speak publicly; Athenian women could not.

The Spartan Marriage Ceremony

The Spartan wedding ceremony was itself unusual. Ancient sources describe a ritual in which the bride’s hair was cut short and she was dressed in men’s clothing and sandals, then left alone in a darkened room for her husband to find. This cross-dressing element puzzled later writers and has been interpreted in various ways — possibly as a transition ritual, marking the passage from one state to another, or as a way of easing the young man’s anxiety about women. Either way, it was strikingly different from the elaborate torch-lit procession of an Athenian wedding. The couple did not live together immediately; the husband continued to sleep in the men’s communal barracks (the syssitia) and visited his wife in secret for some time after the wedding.

Both Athens and Sparta used marriage to serve the needs of the state rather than the wishes of the couple. In Athens, this meant producing legitimate citizen heirs and maintaining household stability. In Sparta, it meant producing strong soldiers. The key analytical point is that in both societies marriage was fundamentally about male political and military concerns; the women’s own desires were largely irrelevant. However, Spartan women gained considerably more freedom and respect as a result of their role — they could own property, speak in public and move around the city. Athenian women were expected to be invisible outside the home.

before.content_html:
The Ideal Athenian Woman

In fifth-century Athens, the ideal woman was barely visible. Pericles, as recorded by Thucydides in his History, is reported to have said that the greatest virtue for a widow is to be spoken of as little as possible among men — whether for good or bad. This striking statement captures the Athenian ideal perfectly: female virtue was defined largely by absence from public life. The ideal Athenian woman was modest, domestic, chaste and silent.

The Kyria and Her Household

Once married, an Athenian woman became the kyria — the mistress of the household. This was her domain. While her husband (the kyrios) represented the family in the public world of the assembly, law courts and markets, the kyria managed everything within the house. This was not a trivial role. She supervised domestic slaves, managed food stores and finances, oversaw weaving and cloth production, and was responsible for the health and upbringing of children. Xenophon’s Oeconomicus (“On Household Management”) is a famous prose dialogue in which a man explains how he trained his wife to run the household efficiently. It presents an idealised picture of the well-ordered oikos (household) and the division of labour between husband and wife — inside versus outside, female versus male.

Key Fact

The kyria managed the oikos: she supervised slaves, controlled food stores, organised weaving and raised children. Her husband handled the public world. The strict division of indoor (female) and outdoor (male) space was fundamental to the Athenian ideal of wifely virtue.

The Gynaikon: Women’s Quarters

The physical layout of the Athenian house reinforced this separation. The gynaikon — the women’s section — was typically located away from the main entrance, often at the back or upper floor of the house, to prevent women from being seen by men arriving or leaving. The andron, the men’s room where the symposium (drinking party) was held, was near the front. Women were not expected to attend symposia. When men entertained male guests, respectable women withdrew.

There is debate among historians about how strictly this seclusion was enforced, and it varied by class. Wealthy women with many slaves could afford to stay indoors; poorer women had to go out to fetch water, visit markets or work in fields. The prescribed material source, the Hegeso Stele (National Archaeological Museum, Athens, no. 3624), depicts a seated woman reaching into a jewellery box held by a standing slave. She is elegantly dressed; her posture is relaxed and domestic. This is the visual image of the ideal kyria: at leisure within her own home, surrounded by the domestic objects and servants that signal her husband’s wealth. There is no suggestion of any public role.

Almost all our written sources about Athenian women were written by men, for male audiences. Funeral speeches, philosophical dialogues and legal speeches give us a male perspective on what women ought to be. Material sources — grave reliefs like the Hegeso Stele and the Ampharete Stele, vase paintings — were also commissioned and created largely by men. This means we see women through the lens of male ideals rather than women’s own voices. The Ampharete Stele (Kerameikos Museum, Athens) is inscribed with the words “I hold here the dear child of my daughter, whom I held on my knees when we were alive and looked on the light of the sun; now dead, I hold it dead.” This is rare evidence of emotional life — but it still comes to us through stone commissioned probably by a male relative.

Weaving and Domestic Virtue

Weaving was the most important skill a respectable Athenian woman could demonstrate. It was both practical — households produced their own cloth — and symbolic: the woman at her loom was the image of domestic virtue. Penelope in Homer’s Odyssey is the literary embodiment of this ideal. She weaves Laertes’ burial shroud by day and unravels it by night to delay the suitors — but the act of weaving itself, repeated daily, signals her virtue and her loyalty to the absent Odysseus. The visual link between weaving and female virtue is confirmed by many Athenian vase paintings showing women at the loom.

Athenian ideas of wifely virtue are summarised by the term aidos — roughly “modesty” or “shame.” A woman with aidos knew her place. She did not draw attention to herself, did not speak to unrelated men, did not appear in public without need. The quality was so valued that Athenian men praised a dead wife in funeral speeches for being someone who was neither seen nor spoken of outside the home.

Key Fact

The Hegeso Stele (c. 400 BC, National Archaeological Museum Athens, no. 3624) shows a seated woman looking at jewellery from a box held by a standing slave. It is a prescribed visual source: it presents the domestic ideal of the kyria — at leisure, at home, surrounded by symbols of wealth and served by a slave.

Domestic Slaves

The running of an Athenian household depended heavily on slaves. Domestic slaves performed the heaviest work: fetching water from the public fountain, cooking, cleaning and laundering. In wealthy households, a trusted female slave might act as a trophos — a nurse or carer who raised the children and held a position of genuine trust within the family. The relationship between mistress and household slave was not straightforwardly cruel or straightforwardly warm; it was a relationship of power in which the slave had no legal autonomy but might nonetheless exercise considerable influence within the domestic space.

The visual culture of Athens frequently places a slave alongside the kyria, as in the Hegeso Stele. This pairing is significant: the presence of the slave reinforces the mistress’s status. A woman without slaves was a poor woman who had to do her own work and was less confined to the house. The Parthenon Frieze (British Museum) also shows women participating in the Panathenaic procession, one of the very few public occasions when respectable women were visible — and even here their role is carefully controlled and religiously framed.

Athenian women were not entirely invisible. They could leave the house to attend religious festivals (such as the Thesmophoria, a women-only festival for Demeter), to visit other women, to attend funerals and to collect water. Religious practice gave women one of their most important public roles: as priestesses, kanephoroi (basket-carriers in processions) and mourners at funerals, women appeared in spaces normally dominated by men. The Parthenon Frieze shows women taking part in the Panathenaic procession, confirming their role in civic religion. But these appearances were bounded by religious necessity; the ideal remained that women were seen as little as possible in everyday life.

practice_questions.text: Read the following summary of a passage from Xenophon's Oeconomicus: A man explains to Socrates that he taught his young wife everything she needed to know when they married. She was not yet fifteen and had lived a sheltered life, seeing and hearing as little as possible. He taught her how to manage the house, supervise the slaves and keep the household stores in order, because these were properly the woman's domain. Using this passage and your wider knowledge, analyse what it reveals about Athenian attitudes to women and domestic life.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): The student uses specific details from the passage (young age at marriage, sheltered upbringing, the man doing the teaching, domestic sphere assigned to the wife) to analyse the power relationship and the assumptions it reveals. They link the passage to the broader Athenian ideal of the kyria: the domestic sphere is the woman's domain but she enters it entirely shaped by male instruction. Strong answers may compare this to the Hegeso Stele as a visual counterpart. Named source cited accurately.

Secure (3–4): Good use of specific details with analytical comments. Some wider context.

Developing (2): Relevant points but largely descriptive.

Emerging (1): A simple point.

practice_questions.text: Explain what the term aidos meant to Athenians and how it shaped the lives of women.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any four of: aidos meant 'modesty' or 'shame'; it was the virtue that prevented a woman from acting in ways that would dishonour herself or her family; in practice it meant a woman did not draw attention to herself in public; it meant not speaking to unrelated men; it meant staying within the domestic space; it was praised in funeral speeches for women who were 'neither seen nor spoken of'; it meant that ideal female behaviour was defined by absence and silence.

practice_questions.text: To what extent did domestic slaves make the Athenian ideal of female seclusion possible? Use named sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): A sustained argument. The student argues that the presence of slaves was essential to the kyria's seclusion: without slaves to fetch water, do heavy work and run errands, the kyria would have had to appear in public. The Hegeso Stele shows the mistress at leisure alongside her slave — the slave's labour enables the mistress's domesticity. For poorer women without slaves, seclusion was impractical. Student may contrast wealthy and poor women's experiences. Named sources used (Hegeso Stele, Ampharete Stele, or Xenophon's Oeconomicus). Clear judgement reached.

Secure (5–6): Clear argument with specific evidence. Named sources used. Judgement.

Developing (3–4): Some relevant points; limited analysis or source use.

Emerging (1–2): Mainly narrative.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Ampharete Stele is similar to or different from the Hegeso Stele as a source of evidence for women's lives in Athens.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (6): Two well-developed points. For example: (1) both are grave reliefs that present women in domestic roles — the Hegeso Stele shows a woman at leisure with jewellery, the Ampharete Stele shows a grandmother holding an infant; both present the female ideal of home and family. (2) The Ampharete Stele includes an inscription giving the woman's own voice ('I hold here the dear child of my daughter'), which makes it unusual as a source since most evidence gives only the male perspective; the Hegeso Stele has no inscription and so provides only visual evidence. Strong answers discuss the limits of both stelai as evidence for real women's inner lives.

Secure (4–5): Two clear points developed with explanation.

Developing (2–3): One well-developed or two underdeveloped points.

Emerging (1): A simple point.

before.content_html:
A Different Kind of Woman

Spartan women were famous throughout the ancient world for their freedom and physical prowess. Other Greeks found them extraordinary — sometimes admirable, sometimes scandalous. Athenian men wrote about Spartan women with a mixture of fascination and disapproval. Aristotle criticised Sparta for allowing women too much licence, arguing that the power of Spartan women undermined the state. Yet Spartan women themselves would not have understood this criticism: their role was entirely shaped by the needs of the polis, and in fulfilling it they earned genuine respect.

Physical Education and Its Purpose

The most striking feature of Spartan female upbringing was its emphasis on physical fitness. Spartan girls ran, wrestled, threw the discus and javelin, and competed in athletic festivals. This was not for its own sake: the entire educational system in Sparta, for both boys and girls, was designed to serve the state’s military needs. Girls were trained to be physically strong because strong, healthy mothers were more likely to survive childbirth and to produce strong sons for the Spartan army.

This was the fundamental logic of Spartan female education: women existed to serve the state’s need for soldiers. They were not trained to be independent; they were trained to be excellent mothers of warriors. But in practice, the physical freedom this required gave Spartan women a much wider range of experience and confidence than their Athenian counterparts. They moved around in public without restriction, spoke their minds and were accustomed to physical activity in mixed-age groups.

Key Fact

Spartan girls received the same physical training as boys — running, wrestling, javelin, discus — to produce fit mothers of warriors. They could own and inherit property, move freely in public, and were expected to manage estates alone while their husbands were away at war.

Property and Independence

Spartan women had property rights that Athenian women entirely lacked. They could own, inherit and manage property in their own right. By the fourth century BC, ancient sources suggest that Spartan women owned approximately two-fifths of Spartan land. This came about partly through accident — the Spartan male citizen population declined dramatically because of warfare losses, leaving estates to female heirs — and partly by design: a Spartan woman needed to be able to manage her husband’s estate when he was absent on campaign or living in the men’s barracks.

This property ownership gave Spartan women a degree of economic independence that was genuinely exceptional in the Greek world. It was also one of the things Aristotle complained about in his Politics. He argued that the wealth of Spartan women made them unwilling to submit to proper discipline, and that their power was a reason for Sparta’s eventual decline. His critique tells us as much about his own Athenian assumptions as it does about Sparta.

Aristotle wrote from an Athenian perspective. In his Politics he argued that the Spartan state had made a fundamental error in neglecting to discipline its women. He saw female freedom as a form of disorder — a state that could not control its women was failing to maintain proper hierarchy. His criticism is useful evidence for how unusual Spartan women appeared to outsiders, but it needs to be used carefully: he was applying Athenian values (female seclusion, male authority) to a society built on entirely different principles. An examiner will reward students who recognise this bias and use it analytically.

The Role of Wife and Mother

The primary role of a Spartan woman was to produce healthy male citizens. Spartan marriage was structured to maximise this. Unlike Athenian men, Spartan husbands did not live with their wives until they were around thirty years old — they slept in the men’s communal barracks (the syssitia). This arrangement meant that the wife managed the household entirely alone. It also gave her genuine authority within the domestic space: she was the effective head of the household in her husband’s absence.

Spartan women were taught to value courage and patriotism. The famous Spartan sayings about mothers — “come back with your shield or on it” — whether historically accurate or not, reflect a cultural ideal: the Spartan mother who did not weep when her son went to war and who would rather see him die gloriously than return as a coward. Ancient sources collected these sayings and attributed them to Spartan women as evidence of their exceptional patriotism and emotional hardness. The Sayings of Spartan Women, preserved by Plutarch in his Moralia, contains dozens of such remarks.

Key Fact

Spartan husbands lived in the men’s communal barracks (syssitia) until around age thirty, even after marriage. This meant Spartan wives managed the household and estate alone — giving them real authority in the domestic space, unlike Athenian women who were supervised by their husbands.

Comparison with the Athenian Woman

The contrast between the Athenian and Spartan woman is one of the most productive analytical topics in this unit. Both societies used women primarily to serve the state’s needs — but they defined those needs very differently. Athens needed women to produce legitimate citizen heirs and maintain household stability; this required control and seclusion. Sparta needed women to produce strong warriors; this required physical training and a degree of independence.

The result was two radically different female experiences. The Athenian kyria was defined by her domesticity and invisibility. The Spartan wife was defined by her physical strength, her ability to manage estates alone and her patriotic dedication to the state. Neither was free in a modern sense — both existed to serve male-defined purposes — but within those purposes the Spartan woman had considerably more agency and respect. Material evidence for Spartan women is sparse compared to Athens: there are no Spartan equivalents of the Hegeso Stele, which itself reflects how differently the two cultures memorialised women.

Spartan women had greater physical freedom, property rights and public visibility than Athenian women. They were not secluded; they participated in public athletic festivals; they could manage estates and speak openly. However, it is important not to romanticise their position: they were trained and managed by the state for the state’s purposes. Their freedom was a tool of Sparta’s military system, not an expression of a belief in gender equality. The key analytical move is to recognise that both Athenian and Spartan societies controlled women — they just did so in different ways and for different ends.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Spartan girls received physical training — running, wrestling, athletics — entirely different from Athenian domestic education, because the Spartan state needed fit mothers to produce strong soldiers.
  • Spartan women could own and inherit property, move freely in public and managed households alone while husbands lived in the syssitia (men’s barracks); Athenian women had none of these rights.
  • Both systems ultimately controlled women for the state’s purposes; the Spartan woman’s greater freedom was a product of military necessity, not a belief in gender equality, and Aristotle’s criticism of Spartan women reveals his own Athenian biases.

Strong answer might argue: clearly Spartan women had more physical freedom (public athletics, no seclusion) and greater economic rights (property ownership). However, both systems controlled women for male purposes — Sparta's control was via military breeding ideology; Athens' via the kyrios system. The student may use Plutarch's Sayings, Aristotle's Politics, the Hegeso Stele (Athens), and comparison of the two marriage systems. A strong judgement recognises the limits of 'freedom' in both cases.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Aristotle's criticism of Spartan women tells us more about Athenian values than about Spartan reality.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (6): Two well-developed points. For example: (1) Aristotle criticised Spartan women for having too much freedom, but this reflects his Athenian assumption that female seclusion and male authority are the natural order — in Sparta, female freedom was not disorder but a deliberate policy to serve military needs; (2) Aristotle blamed Spartan women's wealth for Sparta's decline, but this ignores the military causes of Sparta's reduced citizen population; his critique projects Athenian property norms onto a society where property rules were different by design. Student should recognise Aristotle as a biased source.

Secure (4–5): Two clear points with explanation of Athenian bias.

Developing (2–3): One developed or two undeveloped points.

Emerging (1): A simple point.

before.content_html:
The Roman Matron

In Roman society, the ideal woman was the matrona — the respectable married woman whose life was centred on her family and home. Like the Athenian kyria, the Roman matrona was defined by her domesticity and chastity. But there were important differences. Roman women, particularly those of the upper classes, enjoyed considerably more public visibility than their Athenian counterparts. They attended dinner parties, appeared in public with their husbands and were praised in public funerary inscriptions. The ideals held for them were similar — modesty, chastity, devotion to husband and children — but the Roman social world allowed them to enact those virtues more openly.

The Roman Household: Paterfamilias and Materfamilias

The Roman family was organised around the paterfamilias — the male head of household. In Roman law, the paterfamilias held legal authority (patria potestas) over his wife, children and all household slaves. In theory, this power was absolute. In practice, social expectations and the influence of senior women within the family softened these legal extremes. The woman’s counterpart — the materfamilias — ran the household and raised the children. She was the moral centre of the family.

Roman women’s legal status changed significantly over time. In the early Republic, most women were under the legal authority (manus) of their husband or father. By the late Republic and Imperial period, sine manu marriage had become common: in this arrangement, the wife did not pass into her husband’s legal authority but remained under her father’s — or, if her father was dead, was technically independent. This gave educated, upper-class Roman women a degree of legal agency that Athenian women never possessed.

Key Fact

In early Roman marriage cum manu, a wife passed into her husband’s legal authority. In sine manu marriage (common by the late Republic), she remained under her father’s authority or gained a degree of independence. Sine manu gave upper-class women considerably more legal agency than Athenian women ever held.

Roman Ideals of Female Virtue: Lucretia

The story of Lucretia is the definitive Roman statement of female virtue. Livy narrates the story in History of Rome, 1.57–59. While the Roman princes are away at war, they make a bet about whose wife is most virtuous. They ride back to check. Lucretia alone is found at home, spinning with her slave women by lamplight. The others are at parties. Lucretia wins the bet — but her excellence brings disaster. The prince Sextus Tarquinius is inflamed by her virtue and beauty. He returns alone and threatens to rape her, then to kill her alongside a slave and claim she was caught in adultery. Lucretia yields. The next morning she summons her father and husband, tells them what happened, and stabs herself, saying that although she did not consent, no unchaste woman will ever use her as a precedent.

Her self-inflicted death is the moral climax of the story. In Roman terms, Lucretia is faultless — her body was violated against her will — but she cannot live with the shame of having been violated. Her suicide is an act of the highest virtue: she places the honour of her family and the moral integrity of Roman womanhood above her own survival. Her death so enrages the Romans that they expel the Tarquin dynasty and found the Republic. Lucretia’s body literally founds Roman political freedom.

The Lucretia story reveals that in Roman thinking, female honour was inseparable from female chastity — and that a woman’s chastity was ultimately the property of her male relatives (father, husband) rather than of herself. Lucretia cannot simply be declared innocent and move on; her violation must be cleansed by death. This tells us that the Roman ideal of female virtue was primarily about the reputation and honour of the men connected to the woman, not about the woman’s own wellbeing. Compare this with the Sabine Women, who maintained their honour by serving their families’ interests through self-sacrifice rather than death.

The Laudatio Turiae

The Laudatio Turiae is a prescribed literary source — a long inscription found in Rome, dated to around 8 BC, in which a man praises his wife of over forty years after her death. He praises her for her loyalty, her management of the household during the dangerous years of the civil wars, her attempts to obtain his pardon when he was proscribed, and her offer to divorce him so that he could marry again and have children (since she was childless). He refused, saying he would rather live without children than be parted from her.

The Laudatio Turiae is a rare document: it is a real person’s genuine testimony, not a literary construct. It shows the Roman ideal made real: a wife who was loyal, brave, practical and self-sacrificing. It also shows a husband who valued his wife’s qualities deeply and was willing to say so publicly. This complicates the simple picture of Roman women as passive and voiceless: within marriage, some Roman women clearly exercised real influence and earned genuine respect.

Key Fact

The Laudatio Turiae (c. 8 BC) is a funerary inscription praising a Roman wife for loyalty, bravery during the civil wars and self-sacrificing devotion. It is a prescribed literary source and one of the few surviving direct testimonies to what Roman husbands valued in their wives.

The Pudicitia Ideal in Visual Culture

The Roman ideal of female modesty is embodied in the pudicitia (modesty/chastity) — the central Roman female virtue. The prescribed visual source, the Pudicitia (Pudicizia) statue in the Vatican Museum (Braccio Nuovo 23), shows a draped female figure. She is fully clothed in heavy drapery that covers her from head to toe. Her right hand draws the cloak slightly across her chest in a gesture of modest self-containment. Her head is slightly lowered. There is no display of flesh or adornment; she presents herself as a contained, respectable presence. This posture — covered, self-contained, slightly withdrawn — is the visual language of Roman female virtue.

The so-called “Sappho” fresco, a prescribed visual source from Pompeii, shows a wealthy, educated woman holding a writing tablet and stylus. She is depicted as thoughtful and literate, with carefully styled hair and fine clothing. This contrasts with the Pudicitia statue in an interesting way: the Pompeian fresco suggests that education and intellectual accomplishment were also part of the ideal for wealthy Roman women, at least by the first century AD. Roman women of the upper class received education in reading, writing, music and sometimes rhetoric — a significant difference from the strictly domestic education of most Athenian women.

Both the Roman matrona and the Athenian kyria were defined by chastity, domesticity and devotion to family. But there are important differences. Roman women attended dinner parties alongside their husbands; Athenian women were excluded from the symposium. Roman women of the upper class might receive academic education; Athenian girls were educated only for household management. Roman women under sine manu marriage had greater legal independence than Athenian women, who always required a kyrios. The Laudatio Turiae and the “Sappho” fresco suggest a Roman ideal that valued intelligence and loyalty alongside, not instead of, domestic virtue.

The male head of the Roman household, who held legal authority (patria potestas) over all members of his family including wife, children and slaves.
